tool.name: Matplotlib
tool.tagline: The foundational Python library for static, publication-quality plots
tool.description: Matplotlib is Python's original and most widely used plotting library: it draws line, scatter, bar, image and almost any other 2D chart, and saves them as PNG, SVG or PDF. pandas, seaborn and many scientific tools build on it, so knowing its Figure/Axes model lets you control and fix any chart they produce.

concepts.name: Figures, Axes and pyplot
concepts.summary: The two objects behind every Matplotlib chart: the Figure (the canvas) and the Axes (one plot with its own coordinates).
concepts.why: Every customization you will ever do is a method on a Figure or an Axes, so this mental model makes the rest of the library predictable.
concepts.body:
A Matplotlib chart is a small tree of objects. At the top is the **Figure**: the whole canvas, with a size in inches and a resolution in dots per inch. Inside it live one or more **Axes**: a plotting area with an x axis, a y axis, a title and the data you draw. Note the spelling: an *Axes* is one plot; an *Axis* is one of its two number lines.

The usual entry point is `matplotlib.pyplot`, imported as `plt`. The idiomatic start is:

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
```

which creates a Figure with a single Axes and returns both. You then call methods on `ax` to draw (`ax.plot`, `ax.bar`) and to decorate (`ax.set_title`, `ax.set_xlabel`). Finally you either show the figure in a window or notebook with `plt.show()`, or write it to a file with `fig.savefig("chart.png")`.

- `figsize=(width, height)` is in inches; `dpi` turns inches into pixels when saving a raster image.
- Each Axes has its own data limits, so two side-by-side plots can use different scales.
- pyplot keeps a notion of the "current" figure and axes, which is what the short `plt.plot(...)` style draws on.

When nothing appears, it is usually because the script never called `plt.show()`, or it is running without a display (a server), where you should save to a file instead.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")              # no window needed, e.g. on a server
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16])
ax.set_title("Squares")

print(type(fig).__name__)          # Figure
print(type(ax).__name__)           # Axes
print(fig.get_size_inches())       # [6. 4.]
print(len(fig.axes))               # 1
fig.savefig("squares.png", dpi=100)  # 600 x 400 pixels
takeaways: A Figure is the canvas; an Axes is one plot inside it
`fig, ax = plt.subplots()` is the standard way to start
Draw and decorate by calling methods on `ax`; save with `fig.savefig`
pitfalls: Confusing Axes (a plot) with Axis (the x or y number line).

quiz.q: What does `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` return?
options: Two Axes objects, one per axis
A Figure and a single Axes inside it
A Figure and its x Axis
Only a Figure; ax is None until you plot
quiz.explain: With no arguments subplots creates a 1x1 grid, so you get the Figure plus its one Axes.

concepts.name: Line plots with plot()
concepts.summary: Draw one or more lines from x and y sequences, and control their color, style and markers.
concepts.why: Line plots are the default way to show trends over time or any ordered x, and `plot` is the most used function in the library.
concepts.body:
`ax.plot(x, y)` connects the points `(x[i], y[i])` with straight segments. `x` and `y` can be lists, NumPy arrays or pandas Series of the same length. If you pass only one sequence, it is used as `y` and `x` becomes `0, 1, 2, ...`.

Call `plot` several times on the same Axes to overlay lines; each new line takes the next color from the **property cycle** (blue, orange, green, ...). Style each line with keyword arguments:

- `color="tab:red"` or a hex string like `"#11557C"`.
- `linestyle="--"` (dashed), `":"` (dotted), `"-."`.
- `marker="o"` to draw a symbol at each point, `markersize=4`.
- `linewidth=2`, `alpha=0.6` for transparency.
- `label="train"` so a legend can name the line later.

A compact **format string** such as `"ro--"` (red, circle markers, dashed) is also accepted as the third positional argument; it is handy in quick exploration, but keyword arguments read better in code others maintain.

Smooth-looking curves are just many points: `x = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)` then `ax.plot(x, np.sin(x))`. With too few points you see the straight segments.

`plot` returns a list of `Line2D` objects. Keep a reference (`line, = ax.plot(...)`) if you want to change the line later, for example in an animation.

Line plots assume the x values are ordered. If they are not, the line zigzags back and forth: sort by x first, or use `scatter` for unordered points.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex

x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 100)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, np.sin(x), label="sin")
ax.plot(x, np.cos(x), linestyle="--", color="tab:red", label="cos")
line, = ax.plot(x[::10], np.sin(x[::10]), "ko", markersize=3)

print(len(ax.lines))                  # 3
print(line.get_marker())              # o
print(to_hex(ax.lines[0].get_color()))  # #1f77b4 (first cycle color)
fig.savefig("lines.png")
takeaways: `ax.plot(x, y)` connects points in order; one sequence means y vs index
Repeated calls overlay lines with the next cycle color
Style with `color`, `linestyle`, `marker`, `linewidth`, `label`
pitfalls: Plotting unsorted x values with a line, which produces a zigzag mess.

quiz.q: You call `ax.plot([5, 3, 8])` with a single list. What are the x values?
options: It raises an error: x is required
quiz.explain: With one sequence plot treats it as y and uses the indexes 0..N-1 as x.

concepts.name: Scatter plots
concepts.summary: Show the relationship between two variables as unconnected points, optionally sized and colored by more data.
concepts.why: Scatter plots are the first look at correlation, clusters and outliers in any dataset.
concepts.body:
`ax.scatter(x, y)` draws one marker per point without connecting them, which is what you want when the order of points means nothing. Its power is that size and color can encode two more variables:

- `s=` marker area in points squared, a scalar or one value per point.
- `c=` a single color, or an array of numbers mapped through a **colormap** (`cmap="viridis"`).
- `alpha=` transparency; essential when points overlap heavily.
- `edgecolors="white"` and `linewidths=` to separate touching markers.

When `c` is numeric, `scatter` returns a `PathCollection` that knows its color mapping, so `fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax)` adds a scale explaining the colors.

Note that `s` is an area, not a radius: doubling `s` makes markers look about 1.4 times wider. If you map a variable to `s`, scale it so the smallest values are still visible.

For a single plain color and thousands of points, `ax.plot(x, y, "o", linestyle="none")` is noticeably faster than `scatter`, because it creates one line object instead of a collection with per-point properties. For hundreds of thousands of points, overplotting makes any scatter unreadable; consider `alpha`, a `hexbin` or a 2D histogram instead.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=200)
y = 2 * x + rng.normal(size=200)
size = rng.uniform(10, 80, size=200)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sc = ax.scatter(x, y, s=size, c=y, cmap="viridis", alpha=0.7)
fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label="y value")

print(type(sc).__name__)             # PathCollection
print(sc.get_offsets().shape)        # (200, 2)
print(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1].round(2))  # 0.88 (strong positive)
fig.savefig("scatter.png")
takeaways: Use scatter when point order has no meaning
`s` sets marker area and `c` plus `cmap` maps a variable to color
Add `fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax)` whenever color encodes numbers
pitfalls: Passing a radius-like value to `s`, which is an area, so sizes look exaggerated.

quiz.q: You want marker color to show a numeric 'temperature' column. Which call is right?
quiz.explain: scatter maps a numeric `c` array through a colormap; `color` expects color specs and `s` is size.

concepts.name: Bar charts and histograms
concepts.summary: Compare categories with bar and barh, and show a distribution of values with hist.
concepts.why: Bars and histograms answer the two most common questions about data: how do groups compare, and how are values spread?
concepts.body:
A **bar chart** compares a number across categories. `ax.bar(categories, heights)` accepts strings directly as x positions, and `ax.barh` draws horizontal bars, which are easier to read when category names are long. Useful options: `width=`, `color=`, `edgecolor=`, and `bottom=` to stack one series on top of another.

Grouped bars need a little arithmetic: plot each series at `x - w/2` and `x + w/2` where `x = np.arange(n)`, then set the tick labels to the category names.

A **histogram** is different: it takes raw values, cuts their range into **bins** and counts how many fall in each. `ax.hist(values, bins=30)` returns three things: the counts, the bin edges (one more than the counts) and the bar patches.

- `bins` can be an integer, an explicit list of edges, or a rule such as `"auto"`.
- `density=True` rescales so the bars' total area is 1, which lets you compare samples of different sizes.
- `histtype="step"` draws outlines, good for overlaying two distributions.

The number of bins changes the story a histogram tells: too few hides structure, too many shows noise. Try a few values before drawing conclusions.

Bars encode values by length, so the value axis of a bar chart should start at zero; a truncated axis exaggerates differences. Matplotlib does this by default for bars.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))

langs = ["Python", "Go", "Rust"]
ax1.bar(langs, [42, 18, 12], color="tab:blue")
ax1.set_ylabel("Projects")

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
values = rng.normal(loc=170, scale=8, size=1000)
counts, edges, patches = ax2.hist(values, bins=20, edgecolor="white")

print(len(counts), len(edges))       # 20 21
print(int(counts.sum()))             # 1000
print(ax1.get_ylim()[0])             # 0.0 (bars start at zero)
fig.savefig("bars.png")
takeaways: `bar`/`barh` compare categories; strings work as x positions
`hist` bins raw values and returns counts, edges and patches
Try several bin counts; use `density=True` to compare different-sized samples
pitfalls: Passing already-counted data to `hist`; use `bar` for counts you computed yourself.

quiz.q: `counts, edges, _ = ax.hist(data, bins=10)`. How many values does `edges` hold?
quiz.explain: Ten bins need eleven boundaries: each bin lies between two consecutive edges.

concepts.name: Titles, labels and legends
concepts.summary: Make a chart self-explanatory with a title, axis labels including units, and a legend for multiple series.
concepts.why: A chart without labels and units is a puzzle; these few calls are what makes a plot usable by someone else.
concepts.body:
Three calls cover most labelling: `ax.set_title("...")`, `ax.set_xlabel("...")` and `ax.set_ylabel("...")`. Put units in the axis label, for example `"Latency (ms)"`, so readers do not have to guess. `ax.set(title=..., xlabel=..., ylabel=...)` sets several properties in one call.

A **legend** names each series. Give each plotting call a `label=`, then call `ax.legend()`; only artists with a label appear, and labels starting with an underscore are ignored. Useful options:

- `loc="upper left"` or the default `"best"`, which searches for the emptiest spot (slow with very many points).
- `ncols=2` to lay entries out in columns.
- `frameon=False` for a lighter look.
- `bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1), loc="upper left"` to put the legend outside the plot on the right.

For the whole figure, `fig.suptitle("...")` adds a title above all subplots, and `fig.legend()` builds one legend from every Axes.

Text accepts a subset of **LaTeX-style math** between dollar signs: `ax.set_xlabel(r"$\alpha$ (rad)")`. Use raw strings so backslashes survive.

If labels overlap or get cut off when saving, the fix is layout, not font size: use `layout="constrained"` when creating the figure, or `bbox_inches="tight"` when saving.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

epochs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(layout="constrained")
ax.plot(epochs, [0.9, 0.6, 0.45, 0.4, 0.38], label="train")
ax.plot(epochs, [0.95, 0.7, 0.6, 0.58, 0.6], label="validation")
ax.plot(epochs, [0.5] * 5, "k:", label="_target")   # hidden from legend
ax.set(title="Training loss", xlabel="Epoch", ylabel="Loss")
leg = ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False)

print([t.get_text() for t in leg.get_texts()])  # ['train', 'validation']
print(ax.get_title())                            # Training loss
fig.savefig("loss.png")
takeaways: Label both axes and include units
Give each series `label=` then call `ax.legend()`
Labels starting with `_` are left out of the legend
pitfalls: Calling `ax.legend()` before plotting, or without any `label=`, which gives an empty legend and a warning.

quiz.q: You plotted three lines but only passed `label=` to two of them. What does `ax.legend()` show?
options: Two entries, for the labelled lines
Nothing until all lines have labels
quiz.explain: Only artists with a label (not starting with an underscore) are collected into the legend.

concepts.name: Grids of plots with subplots
concepts.summary: Create several Axes in a grid with plt.subplots(nrows, ncols) and share axes between them.
concepts.why: Small multiples, comparing panels side by side, are one of the clearest ways to show data, and they all start here.
concepts.body:
`plt.subplots(nrows, ncols)` creates a Figure with a grid of Axes. What it returns depends on the shape:

- `1, 1` (the default): a single Axes object.
- one row or one column: a 1D NumPy array of Axes, which you can unpack: `fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2)`.
- a real grid: a 2D array indexed as `axs[row, col]`.

Passing `squeeze=False` always returns a 2D array, which is handy in code that builds grids of variable size. To loop over every Axes regardless of shape, use `axs.flat`.

`sharex=True` or `sharey=True` links the limits of the panels, so zooming or setting a limit on one applies to all, and inner tick labels are hidden to save space. Use `"row"` or `"col"` to share only along rows or columns. Shared axes are what make panels honestly comparable.

`figsize` is the size of the whole figure, so make it larger as you add panels. Combine with `layout="constrained"` so titles and tick labels of neighboring panels do not collide.

Empty cells, for instance seven plots in a 2x4 grid, can be hidden with `axs[1, 3].set_axis_off()` or removed with `fig.delaxes`. For unequal sizes, such as one wide plot above two small ones, move on to `subplot_mosaic` or GridSpec.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 1, 50)
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(9, 5), sharex=True, sharey=True,
                        layout="constrained")
print(axs.shape)                       # (2, 3)

for k, ax in enumerate(axs.flat[:5]):
    ax.plot(x, x ** (k + 1))
    ax.set_title(f"x^{k + 1}")
axs[1, 2].set_axis_off()               # hide the unused sixth panel

axs[0, 0].set_ylim(0, 2)               # shared: applies to every panel
print([float(v) for v in axs[1, 1].get_ylim()])  # [0.0, 2.0]
fig.savefig("grid.png")
takeaways: `plt.subplots(r, c)` returns a scalar, 1D or 2D array of Axes depending on shape
Iterate with `axs.flat`; index grids as `axs[row, col]`
`sharex`/`sharey` make panels directly comparable
pitfalls: Indexing `axs[0]` on a 2D grid and getting a whole row instead of one Axes.

quiz.q: `fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3)`. What is `axs`?
options: A 1D NumPy array of three Axes
A single Axes with three panels
quiz.explain: With one row subplots squeezes the result to a 1D array of length 3.

concepts.name: Saving figures to files
concepts.summary: Export figures as PNG, SVG or PDF with savefig, and control resolution, margins and transparency.
concepts.why: Charts end up in reports, papers and web pages, and the right format and resolution decide whether they look crisp or blurry.
concepts.body:
`fig.savefig("name.ext")` writes the figure, and the extension picks the format. Choose by destination:

- **PNG**: raster, good for web pages, slides and screenshots. Set `dpi=` (dots per inch); pixel size is `figsize` times `dpi`, so a 6x4 inch figure at 200 dpi is 1200x800 pixels.
- **SVG** and **PDF**: vector, so they scale without blurring; best for papers and print. Text stays text and file sizes stay small for simple plots, but huge scatter plots make large vector files.
- JPEG is supported (with Pillow) but blurs sharp lines; avoid it for charts.

Other useful arguments:

- `bbox_inches="tight"` crops surrounding whitespace and includes labels that would otherwise be clipped.
- `pad_inches=` controls the margin left by the tight crop.
- `transparent=True` makes the background transparent, useful for slides with colored backgrounds.
- `facecolor=` sets the background color explicitly.

Fonts and line widths are specified in points, which are physical units. If text looks tiny in a saved image, the figure is too large in inches for its intended display size; reduce `figsize` instead of increasing every font.

Call `savefig` before `plt.show()` in scripts: after the window is closed, pyplot may have discarded the figure and you would save a blank image. In loops that create many figures, `plt.close(fig)` after saving releases the memory.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))
ax.plot([0, 1, 2], [2, 0, 1])
ax.set_ylabel("A label that might be clipped")

fig.savefig("chart.png", dpi=150)
fig.savefig("chart_tight.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
fig.savefig("chart.svg")                 # vector, scales freely
plt.close(fig)                           # free memory in loops

print(Image.open("chart.png").size)      # (600, 450) = 4x3 in * 150 dpi
print(Image.open("chart_tight.png").size[0] < 600)  # True: whitespace cropped
takeaways: The file extension picks the format: PNG for screens, SVG/PDF for print
Pixel size = figsize (inches) x dpi
`bbox_inches='tight'` crops whitespace and avoids clipped labels
pitfalls: Saving after `plt.show()` in a script and getting an empty image.

quiz.q: A 5x3 inch figure is saved with `dpi=200`. How large is the PNG?
options: It depends on the screen resolution
quiz.explain: Pixel dimensions are inches times dots per inch: 5*200 by 3*200.

concepts.name: pyplot vs the object-oriented API
concepts.summary: Understand the implicit pyplot state machine and the explicit Axes-method style, and when to use each.
concepts.why: Most confusing Matplotlib bugs come from mixing the two interfaces; knowing both lets you read any example online.
concepts.body:
Matplotlib has two interfaces that draw the same things.

The **implicit pyplot** interface keeps hidden global state: a current Figure and a current Axes. `plt.plot`, `plt.title`, `plt.xlabel` all act on whichever Axes is current, and `plt.subplot(2, 1, 2)` changes which one that is. It is short and fine for a quick look in a notebook.

The **explicit object-oriented** interface creates objects and calls methods on them: `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` then `ax.plot`, `ax.set_title`, `ax.set_xlabel`. Nothing depends on what was created last, so it scales to multiple panels and to reusable functions. The official guidance is to prefer it for anything beyond throwaway code.

Names differ slightly between the two: `plt.title` is `ax.set_title`, `plt.xlim` is `ax.set_xlim`, `plt.xticks` is `ax.set_xticks`. The pyplot versions are thin wrappers that call `plt.gca()` (get current Axes) and then the method.

A good pattern for reusable plotting code is a function that accepts an Axes:

```python
def plot_series(ax, x, y, **kw):
    return ax.plot(x, y, **kw)
```

The caller decides where the plot goes, so the same function works in a one-off chart or one panel of a grid. This is exactly how pandas and seaborn accept `ax=`.

Still use `pyplot` for figure creation (`plt.subplots`, `plt.figure`), `plt.show()` and `plt.close()`: those manage windows and memory.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Implicit: acts on the "current" Axes
plt.figure()
plt.plot([1, 2, 3])
plt.title("implicit")
print(plt.gca().get_title())          # implicit

# Explicit: methods on objects you hold
def plot_series(ax, ys, **kw):
    ax.plot(ys, **kw)
    ax.set_title(kw.get("label", ""))
    return ax

fig, (a, b) = plt.subplots(1, 2)
plot_series(a, [3, 1, 2], label="left")
plot_series(b, [1, 1, 4], label="right")
print([ax.get_title() for ax in fig.axes])  # ['left', 'right']
print(plt.gca() is b)                 # True: last Axes created is "current"
plt.close("all")
takeaways: pyplot functions act on the current Axes; OO methods act on the object you hold
Prefer `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` and `ax.` methods in real code
Write plotting helpers that take an `ax` argument
pitfalls: Calling `plt.title()` in a multi-panel figure and titling the wrong panel.

quiz.q: Which explicit-API call is equivalent to `plt.xlim(0, 10)`?
quiz.explain: Most setters on the Axes are spelled set_<property>; pyplot drops the set_ prefix.

concepts.name: Colors, markers and style sheets
concepts.summary: Specify colors in every supported way, use the property cycle, and switch the whole look with style sheets.
concepts.why: Consistent, accessible colors make charts readable, and style sheets let you change a whole report's look in one line.
concepts.body:
Matplotlib accepts colors in many forms:

- named colors: `"red"`, `"steelblue"`;
- the Tableau palette used by default: `"tab:blue"`, `"tab:orange"` ...;
- hex strings `"#11557C"` or RGB(A) tuples of floats `(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8)`;
- `"C0"`, `"C1"` ... meaning the nth color of the current **property cycle**;
- a grayscale string such as `"0.6"`.

When you do not pass a color, each new line or bar group takes the next entry of the cycle. Using `"C0"` explicitly lets you match a line and its shaded band without hard-coding a value.

Markers (`"o"`, `"s"`, `"^"`, `"x"`, `"."`), line styles (`"-"`, `"--"`, `":"`) and widths complete the look. Redundant encoding, such as color plus marker or line style, keeps charts readable in grayscale and for color-blind readers.

**Style sheets** change many defaults at once: fonts, grid, colors, background. `plt.style.available` lists the built-ins (`"ggplot"`, `"seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid"`, `"fivethirtyeight"`, `"tableau-colorblind10"` ...). Apply one globally with `plt.style.use("ggplot")`, or temporarily:

```python
with plt.style.context("dark_background"):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
```

Styles are applied when artists are created, so switch style before making the figure, not after.

For colors that encode numbers, do not hand-pick: use a **colormap**, covered with images and heatmaps.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex

print(to_hex("tab:blue"), to_hex("C1"))  # #1f77b4 #ff7f0e
print(to_hex((0.0, 0.5, 1.0)))           # #0080ff
print("ggplot" in plt.style.available)   # True

with plt.style.context("tableau-colorblind10"):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    for k, m in enumerate(["o", "s", "^"]):
        ax.plot([0, 1, 2], [k, k + 1, k + 0.5], marker=m, label=f"series {k}")
    print(to_hex(ax.lines[0].get_color()))  # #006ba4 (from that style's cycle)
    ax.legend()
    fig.savefig("styled.png")
takeaways: Colors can be names, `tab:` colors, hex, RGB tuples or cycle refs `C0`..`C9`
Encode series with color plus marker or line style for accessibility
`plt.style.context(...)` applies a style sheet temporarily; set it before creating the figure
pitfalls: Switching style after creating a figure and expecting existing artists to change.

quiz.q: You plot a line without a color and want a shaded band in exactly the same color. What is the simplest choice?
options: Use `color='C0'` for both if it is the first line
quiz.explain: 'C0' refers to the first color of the active cycle, which is what the first unstyled line received.

concepts.name: Limits, ticks and tick formatting
concepts.summary: Control axis ranges, tick positions and tick label formats with set_xlim, locators and formatters.
concepts.why: Default ticks are often fine but wrong for percentages, currency or categories; precise control is what makes charts publication-ready.
concepts.body:
**Limits** come from the data plus a small margin. Override them with `ax.set_xlim(left, right)` and `ax.set_ylim(bottom, top)`; pass `None` for one side to keep it automatic. Reversing the order, `set_ylim(10, 0)`, flips the axis. `ax.margins(0)` removes the padding.

**Ticks** are chosen by a **locator** and labelled by a **formatter**, both attached to each `Axis` (`ax.xaxis`, `ax.yaxis`).

Quick, explicit control:

```python
ax.set_xticks([0, 5, 10], labels=["start", "middle", "end"])
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45, labelsize=8)
```

Rule-based control, which keeps working when data changes:

- `ticker.MultipleLocator(5)`: a tick every 5 units.
- `ticker.MaxNLocator(nbins=4, integer=True)`: at most a few integer ticks.
- `ticker.PercentFormatter(xmax=1)`: shows 0.25 as 25%.
- `ticker.StrMethodFormatter("{x:,.0f}")`: thousands separators.
- `ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda v, pos: ...)`: anything you can compute.

Set them with `ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(...)` and `ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(...)`. Passing a format string directly, `ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter("{x:.1f} s")`, creates a `StrMethodFormatter` for you.

Minor ticks are off by default for linear axes; `ax.minorticks_on()` adds them. A light grid, `ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)`, helps readers look up values.

Hard-coded tick labels via `set_xticks(labels=...)` are tied to fixed positions. If the limits change later, they will no longer match; prefer a formatter when the labels are derived from values.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import ticker

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([0, 1, 2, 3], [0.12, 0.35, 0.61, 0.9])
ax.set_xlim(0, 3)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(ticker.MultipleLocator(1))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.PercentFormatter(xmax=1))
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

fig.canvas.draw()                     # ticks are computed at draw time
print([t.get_text() for t in ax.get_yticklabels()][:3])  # ['0%', '20%', '40%']
fig.savefig("ticks.png")
takeaways: `set_xlim`/`set_ylim` set ranges; reversed limits flip an axis
Locators choose tick positions, formatters choose their labels
Prefer formatters over hard-coded labels when labels derive from values
pitfalls: Setting fixed tick labels and then changing limits, leaving labels that no longer match positions.

quiz.q: Your y values are fractions from 0 to 1 and you want labels like '40%'. What should you use?
options: Multiply the data by 100 and add '%' to the title
quiz.explain: A formatter changes the labels only; PercentFormatter with xmax=1 maps 0.4 to 40%.

concepts.name: Log scales and twin axes
concepts.summary: Plot data spanning orders of magnitude on log or symlog scales, and overlay two y scales with twinx.
concepts.why: Growth, latency and frequency data often span decades, where a linear axis hides everything but the largest values.
concepts.body:
`ax.set_yscale("log")` (or `ax.set_xscale`) spaces ticks by powers of ten, so equal distances mean equal ratios. Exponential growth becomes a straight line, and small and huge values are both visible. `ax.loglog`, `ax.semilogy` and `ax.semilogx` are shortcuts that plot and set scales at once.

Log scales cannot show zero or negative values. By default those points are masked (not drawn). If your data crosses zero, use:

- `"symlog"`: linear within `linthresh` of zero and logarithmic beyond, symmetric for negatives.
- `"asinh"`: a smooth alternative with similar behavior.
- `"logit"` for probabilities very close to 0 or 1.

A **twin axis** shares the x axis but has an independent y axis on the right: `ax2 = ax.twinx()`. Use it to overlay, say, temperature and rainfall over the same months. Each Axes has its own lines, so a combined legend needs the handles from both:

```python
h1, l1 = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
h2, l2 = ax2.get_legend_handles_labels()
ax.legend(h1 + h2, l1 + l2)
```

Color each y axis label like its line so readers know which scale applies.

Use twin axes sparingly: two independent scales let a chart suggest correlations that depend only on how you set the limits. Side-by-side subplots with a shared x are often more honest.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

days = np.arange(1, 31)
users = 10 * 1.3 ** days

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(days, users, color="C0", label="users")
ax.set_yscale("log")                          # exponential -> straight line
ax.set_ylabel("Users (log)", color="C0")

ax2 = ax.twinx()                               # second y axis, same x
ax2.plot(days, np.gradient(users) / users * 100, "C1--", label="growth %")
ax2.set_ylabel("Daily growth (%)", color="C1")

h1, l1 = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
h2, l2 = ax2.get_legend_handles_labels()
ax.legend(h1 + h2, l1 + l2, loc="upper left")
print(ax.get_yscale(), ax2.get_yscale())       # log linear
fig.savefig("growth.png")
takeaways: Log scales show ratios; exponential growth becomes linear
Use symlog or asinh when data includes zero or negatives
`ax.twinx()` adds an independent right y axis; merge legends manually
pitfalls: Plotting zeros on a log axis and silently losing those points.

quiz.q: Your data includes zeros and values up to one million. Which scale shows all of it with log-like spacing for large values?
quiz.explain: symlog is linear near zero and logarithmic beyond linthresh, so zero is representable.

concepts.name: Images, heatmaps and colormaps
concepts.summary: Display 2D arrays with imshow and pcolormesh, pick a perceptually uniform colormap, and add a colorbar.
concepts.why: Correlation matrices, images and gridded data are all 2D arrays, and a well-chosen colormap is the difference between insight and illusion.
concepts.body:
`ax.imshow(A)` draws a 2D array as a grid of colored pixels. Three behaviors to know:

- Row 0 is at the **top** by default (image convention). Pass `origin="lower"` for matrices that should read like a graph.
- The aspect ratio is fixed so pixels are square; `aspect="auto"` lets the image fill the Axes.
- 3D arrays of shape `(rows, cols, 3)` or `(..., 4)` are treated as RGB(A) images, not mapped through a colormap.

`ax.pcolormesh(X, Y, C)` draws a grid of quadrilaterals with arbitrary, possibly uneven coordinates, which suits scientific grids better than pixel positions.

Values are mapped to colors by a **norm** and a **colormap**. `vmin`/`vmax` fix the range so several panels share a scale. Choose the colormap by data type:

- sequential (`"viridis"`, `"magma"`, `"cividis"`): ordered values from low to high;
- diverging (`"RdBu_r"`, `"coolwarm"`): values around a meaningful center like 0; pair with `vmin=-m, vmax=m` or `colors.CenteredNorm()`;
- qualitative (`"tab10"`): categories, not magnitudes.

Avoid `"jet"` and rainbow maps: their uneven brightness creates fake boundaries and they fail in grayscale.

Always add `fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax)`; without it the colors have no meaning. For annotated heatmaps (numbers in each cell), loop over the cells with `ax.text`, or let seaborn's `heatmap` do it.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
data = rng.normal(size=(200, 4))
data[:, 1] += data[:, 0]                  # make columns 0 and 1 correlated
corr = np.corrcoef(data, rowvar=False)    # 4 x 4 matrix

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
im = ax.imshow(corr, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="correlation")
ax.set_xticks(range(4), labels=list("ABCD"))
ax.set_yticks(range(4), labels=list("ABCD"))
for i in range(4):
    for j in range(4):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{corr[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)

print(corr.shape, round(corr[0, 1], 2))  # (4, 4) 0.72
print(im.get_clim())                     # (-1.0, 1.0)
fig.savefig("corr.png")
takeaways: `imshow` puts row 0 at the top; use `origin='lower'` for graph-like matrices
Sequential maps for magnitudes, diverging maps centred on a meaningful value
Fix `vmin`/`vmax` to compare panels, and always add a colorbar
pitfalls: Using a rainbow colormap such as jet, which invents visual boundaries.

quiz.q: You plot a correlation matrix (values from -1 to 1). Which setup is most appropriate?
quiz.explain: Correlation has a meaningful center at 0, so a diverging map with symmetric limits fits.

concepts.name: Text, annotations and bar labels
concepts.summary: Point out what matters with ax.text, ax.annotate arrows, reference lines and automatic bar labels.
concepts.why: Annotations turn a chart into an argument by telling readers exactly where to look.
concepts.body:
`ax.text(x, y, "label")` places text at data coordinates. Align it with `ha` (horizontal: `"left"`, `"center"`, `"right"`) and `va`. To place text relative to the Axes box rather than the data, for example in the top-left corner regardless of limits, add `transform=ax.transAxes` and use coordinates between 0 and 1.

`ax.annotate` draws text with an optional arrow:

```python
ax.annotate("peak", xy=(x0, y0), xytext=(x0 + 1, y0 + 2),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
```

`xy` is the point being annotated and `xytext` where the text sits. `textcoords="offset points"` makes `xytext` an offset in points, which keeps the label a fixed visual distance away however the data is scaled.

Reference lines and spans mark thresholds and periods:

- `ax.axhline(y)` and `ax.axvline(x)` span the whole Axes;
- `ax.axhspan(y0, y1)` and `ax.axvspan(x0, x1, alpha=0.2)` shade a band;
- `ax.fill_between(x, low, high, alpha=0.3)` shades between curves, ideal for confidence bands.

For bar charts, `ax.bar_label(bars)` writes each bar's value on or above it; `fmt="{:.1f}"` and `padding=3` adjust the format and spacing, and `label_type="center"` puts labels inside stacked segments.

Restraint matters: one or two annotations make a point, ten create clutter.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5), layout="constrained")

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
y = np.sin(x) * np.exp(-x / 5)
i = y.argmax()
ax1.plot(x, y)
ax1.annotate("peak", xy=(x[i], y[i]), xytext=(20, -20),
             textcoords="offset points", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
ax1.axhline(0, color="gray", linewidth=0.8)
ax1.axvspan(6, 8, alpha=0.15, color="C1")
ax1.text(0.02, 0.95, "damped", transform=ax1.transAxes, va="top")

bars = ax2.bar(["Q1", "Q2", "Q3"], [12.5, 18.25, 9.0])
labels = ax2.bar_label(bars, fmt="{:.1f}", padding=3)
print([t.get_text() for t in labels])   # ['12.5', '18.2', '9.0']
fig.savefig("annotated.png")
takeaways: `ax.text` places text; `transform=ax.transAxes` uses 0..1 Axes coordinates
`ax.annotate(text, xy=point, xytext=..., arrowprops=...)` points at data
`axhline`, `axvspan`, `fill_between` and `bar_label` cover most chart callouts
pitfalls: Positioning text in data coordinates that later fall outside the limits, so the label silently disappears.

quiz.q: You want a note fixed in the top-right corner of the plot no matter how the data limits change. What do you use?
quiz.explain: transAxes coordinates run from 0 to 1 across the Axes box, independent of data limits.

concepts.name: Time series, error bars and bands
concepts.summary: Plot datetime x axes with readable date ticks and show uncertainty with errorbar and fill_between.
concepts.why: Most real data is a time series, and a value without its uncertainty can mislead.
concepts.body:
Matplotlib understands `datetime`, `numpy.datetime64` and pandas timestamps on either axis: pass them to `plot` directly. It converts them to floating-point days internally and picks date-aware ticks.

To control the ticks, use the date locators and formatters from `matplotlib.dates`:

- `mdates.MonthLocator()`, `WeekdayLocator()`, `DayLocator(interval=7)` choose positions;
- `mdates.DateFormatter("%b %Y")` formats with strftime codes;
- `mdates.ConciseDateFormatter(locator)` produces compact, non-repetitive labels (year shown only when it changes) and is usually the best default.

`fig.autofmt_xdate()` rotates and right-aligns crowded date labels.

For **uncertainty**:

- `ax.errorbar(x, y, yerr=err, fmt="o", capsize=3)` draws points with error bars; `yerr` can be a scalar, one value per point, or a 2xN array for asymmetric errors (below, above).
- `ax.fill_between(x, low, high, alpha=0.25)` draws a shaded band, which reads better than error bars for dense series such as forecasts or rolling statistics.

Say in the caption or legend what the bars mean: one standard deviation, standard error and a 95% confidence interval differ by large factors.

With pandas, `df.plot()` already uses these mechanisms; any formatter you set afterwards on `ax.xaxis` still applies.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import numpy as np

days = np.arange("2026-01-01", "2026-04-01", dtype="datetime64[D]")
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
y = np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=days.size))
err = 1.0 + 0.02 * np.arange(days.size)       # uncertainty grows over time

fig, ax = plt.subplots(layout="constrained")
ax.plot(days, y, color="C0")
ax.fill_between(days, y - err, y + err, color="C0", alpha=0.25)
loc = mdates.MonthLocator()
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(loc)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.ConciseDateFormatter(loc))

fig.canvas.draw()
print(days.size)                               # 90
print([t.get_text() for t in ax.get_xticklabels()])  # ['2026', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr']
fig.savefig("ts.png")
takeaways: Pass datetimes straight to `plot`; Matplotlib picks date ticks
`ConciseDateFormatter` gives compact, readable date labels
Use `errorbar` for sparse points and `fill_between` bands for dense series
pitfalls: Showing error bars without stating whether they are standard deviation, standard error or a confidence interval.

quiz.q: You have a daily forecast for a year with a lower and upper bound per day. What is the clearest way to show the bounds?
options: ax.errorbar with capsize=5 on every point
quiz.explain: With hundreds of points, a shaded band is far more readable than hundreds of error bars.

concepts.name: Complex layouts: constrained, mosaic, GridSpec
concepts.summary: Build uneven multi-panel figures with subplot_mosaic and GridSpec, and let constrained layout prevent overlaps.
concepts.why: Dashboards and paper figures rarely fit a uniform grid, and manual spacing tweaks break whenever labels change.
concepts.body:
**Constrained layout** (`layout="constrained"` in `plt.subplots` or `plt.figure`) adjusts Axes positions at draw time so titles, labels, colorbars and legends fit without overlapping. It replaces calling `fig.tight_layout()` after the fact and handles colorbars and figure legends better. Tune spacing with `fig.get_layout_engine().set(w_pad=..., h_pad=..., wspace=..., hspace=...)`.

`fig.subplot_mosaic` describes a layout with a picture:

```python
axd = fig.subplot_mosaic([["top", "top"],
                          ["left", "right"]])
```

Repeating a label makes that Axes span those cells. Use `"."` for an empty cell. The result is a dict keyed by label, which is more readable than array indexes. A string shorthand works too: `"AAB;CCB"` uses `;` between rows. `width_ratios` and `height_ratios` set relative sizes.

**GridSpec** is the lower-level tool: `gs = fig.add_gridspec(3, 3)` then `fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :])` takes the full top row and `gs[1:, :2]` a 2x2 block. Nested grids come from `gs[0].subgridspec(2, 2)`.

**Subfigures** (`fig.subfigures(1, 2)`) split a figure into independent regions, each with its own suptitle, colorbar and layout, which is useful when the left half is a grid of images and the right half a single chart.

Constrained layout is not compatible with manual `fig.subplots_adjust`; choose one or the other.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6), layout="constrained")
axd = fig.subplot_mosaic(
    [["trend", "trend", "hist"],
     ["map",   "map",   "hist"],
     ["map",   "map",   "."]],
    width_ratios=[1, 1, 0.8],
)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
axd["trend"].plot(rng.normal(size=100).cumsum())
axd["hist"].hist(rng.normal(size=500), orientation="horizontal")
im = axd["map"].imshow(rng.random((20, 30)), aspect="auto")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axd["map"])
for name, ax in axd.items():
    ax.set_title(name)

print(sorted(axd))                     # ['hist', 'map', 'trend']
print(type(fig.get_layout_engine()).__name__)  # ConstrainedLayoutEngine
fig.savefig("mosaic.png")
takeaways: `layout='constrained'` prevents overlaps, including with colorbars
`subplot_mosaic` draws a layout from a picture and returns a dict of Axes
GridSpec slices and subfigures cover nested and spanning layouts
pitfalls: Combining constrained layout with `subplots_adjust`, which disables or fights the engine.

quiz.q: In `fig.subplot_mosaic([['a', 'a'], ['b', 'c']])`, what is Axes 'a'?
options: One Axes spanning the whole top row
An error: labels must be unique
One Axes in the top-left cell only
quiz.explain: Repeating a label in adjacent cells makes one Axes that spans those cells.

concepts.name: rcParams and building a house style
concepts.summary: Change Matplotlib defaults through rcParams, write your own .mplstyle file, and scope changes with rc_context.
concepts.why: Teams want every chart to share fonts, sizes and colors without repeating twenty keyword arguments in every plot.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib as mpl
mpl.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from cycler import cycler
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex
from pathlib import Path

Path("house.mplstyle").write_text(
    "axes.spines.top: False\n"
    "axes.spines.right: False\n"
    "axes.grid: True\n"
    "font.size: 11\n"
)
plt.style.use("./house.mplstyle")
print(mpl.rcParams["axes.spines.top"], mpl.rcParams["font.size"])  # False 11.0

with mpl.rc_context({"axes.prop_cycle": cycler(color=["#11557C", "#E8A33D"])}):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot([1, 2]); ax.plot([2, 1])
    print([l.get_color() for l in ax.lines])  # ['#11557C', '#E8A33D']

print(to_hex(mpl.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"].by_key()["color"][0]))  # #1f77b4
takeaways: rcParams hold every default and are read when artists are created
Use `rc_context` for local changes and `.mplstyle` files for a team style
Styles compose in order; `rcdefaults()` resets everything
pitfalls: Changing rcParams after creating a figure and expecting existing text and lines to update.

quiz.q: You need 8-point fonts only for one helper that creates a small figure. What is the cleanest approach?
options: mpl.rcParams['font.size'] = 8 at the top of the module
Edit matplotlibrc in the config directory
Wrap the figure creation in `with mpl.rc_context({'font.size': 8}):`
quiz.explain: rc_context scopes the change to the block and restores the previous values afterwards.

concepts.name: Backends, interactive mode and notebooks
concepts.summary: Learn how backends render and display figures, how to run headless, and how plt.show and interactive mode behave.
concepts.why: Blank windows, frozen scripts and 'cannot connect to display' errors all come from backend choices you can control.
concepts.body:
A **backend** is the part of Matplotlib that turns a Figure into pixels or a file and, optionally, shows it in a window. There are two kinds:

- **Non-interactive** (renderers only): `Agg` for PNG, plus `pdf`, `svg`, `ps`. Use these on servers, in CI and in batch jobs.
- **Interactive**: GUI backends such as `QtAgg`, `TkAgg`, `MacOSX` and `GTK4Agg`, which open windows with pan and zoom; and notebook backends: `inline` (static PNGs, the default in Jupyter) and `ipympl`'s `widget` backend (interactive figures inside the notebook, enabled with `%matplotlib widget`).

Matplotlib picks a default automatically and falls back to `Agg` when no display is available. Override with `matplotlib.use("Agg")` before creating figures, the `MPLBACKEND` environment variable, or the `backend` rcParam. `matplotlib.get_backend()` reports the current one.

`plt.show()` in a script **blocks** until all windows are closed. In an interactive session, `plt.ion()` turns on interactive mode: figures appear immediately and update on each pyplot call, and `show` does not block. `plt.pause(0.1)` runs the GUI event loop briefly, the simplest way to update a live plot in a loop.

pyplot keeps a reference to every figure it created until you close it. In long-running programs that generate many charts, call `plt.close(fig)`; otherwise memory grows and Matplotlib warns once more than 20 figures are open. Alternatively, create figures with `matplotlib.figure.Figure()` directly, which pyplot never tracks.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")                 # must be before any figure is shown
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.figure import Figure

print(matplotlib.get_backend())       # Agg

for i in range(30):                   # batch job: always close
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot([0, i])
    fig.savefig(f"chart_{i}.png")
    plt.close(fig)
print(len(plt.get_fignums()))         # 0: nothing kept alive

# A Figure created directly is never tracked by pyplot
fig = Figure(figsize=(3, 2))
ax = fig.subplots()
ax.bar(["a", "b"], [1, 3])
fig.savefig("untracked.png")
print(len(plt.get_fignums()))         # 0
takeaways: Agg and other non-interactive backends render to files; GUI and notebook backends display
Select a backend with `matplotlib.use`, `MPLBACKEND` or rcParams
Close figures in loops, or use `Figure()` directly in servers
pitfalls: Using pyplot in a web server without closing figures, leaking memory on every request.

quiz.q: A Flask endpoint renders a PNG chart per request using pyplot and memory keeps growing. What is the most likely fix?
options: Close each figure with plt.close(fig), or build it with Figure() instead of pyplot
quiz.explain: pyplot keeps every figure alive until closed; Figure() objects are garbage collected normally.

concepts.name: Animations with FuncAnimation
concepts.summary: Animate a figure frame by frame with FuncAnimation and export it as GIF or MP4.
concepts.why: Animations explain processes that unfold over time, such as simulations and training curves, better than static frames.
concepts.body:
`matplotlib.animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=..., interval=...)` repeatedly calls your `update(frame)` function and redraws the figure. The efficient pattern is to create artists once and only change their data in `update`:

```python
line, = ax.plot([], [])
def update(i):
    line.set_data(x[:i], y[:i])
    return (line,)
```

Setting data on existing artists is much faster than clearing the Axes and plotting again. Because empty initial artists do not set limits, fix them yourself with `set_xlim` and `set_ylim`.

- `frames` can be an integer (passes 0..n-1), any iterable, or a generator function.
- `interval` is the delay between frames in milliseconds for on-screen playback.
- `blit=True` redraws only the artists `update` returns, a big speedup on interactive backends; then `update` must return an iterable of artists.

Keep a reference to the animation object (`anim = FuncAnimation(...)`). If it is garbage collected, the animation silently stops.

To export, call `anim.save("out.gif", writer="pillow", fps=20)` (needs Pillow only) or `anim.save("out.mp4", writer="ffmpeg")` (needs the ffmpeg program). In Jupyter, `HTML(anim.to_jshtml())` embeds a player without any external tool.

For a handful of precomputed images, `ArtistAnimation` takes a list of artist lists, one per frame, instead of a function.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 120)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))
ax.set_xlim(0, 2 * np.pi)
ax.set_ylim(-1.1, 1.1)
line, = ax.plot([], [], lw=2)
calls = []

def update(i):
    calls.append(i)
    line.set_data(x[:i], np.sin(x[:i]))   # change data, don't replot
    return (line,)

anim = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(x), interval=30, blit=True)
anim.save("wave.gif", writer="pillow", fps=30)
print(calls[-1])                      # 119: last frame index
print(len(line.get_xdata()))          # 119
takeaways: Create artists once; update their data in the frame function
Fix axis limits yourself, and return the changed artists when `blit=True`
Keep a reference to the animation; save with the pillow (GIF) or ffmpeg (MP4) writer
pitfalls: Not storing the FuncAnimation in a variable, so it is garbage collected and nothing animates.

quiz.q: Why is `line.set_data(...)` preferred over `ax.clear(); ax.plot(...)` inside the update function?
options: set_data reuses the existing artist, avoiding rebuilding the Axes on every frame
ax.clear is not allowed in animations
plot cannot be called more than once per Axes
set_data also saves the frame to disk
quiz.explain: Recreating artists and resetting the Axes each frame is far slower and also resets titles and limits.

concepts.name: The Artist hierarchy
concepts.summary: See every visible element as an Artist in a tree under the Figure, and find, inspect and modify any of them.
concepts.why: When no keyword argument does what you need, walking the Artist tree lets you change any detail of any chart, including those made by pandas or seaborn.
concepts.body:
Everything drawn in Matplotlib is an **Artist**. The tree looks like this:

- `Figure` contains Axes, figure-level text, legends and patches (the background `fig.patch`).
- `Axes` contains its two `Axis` objects (with `Tick`s, which hold `Line2D` tick marks and `Text` labels), `spines`, the title texts and the data artists in `ax.lines`, `ax.patches`, `ax.collections`, `ax.images` and `ax.texts`.

Primitives are `Line2D`, `Rectangle` and other `Patch`es, `Text`, `AxesImage` and `Collection`s (many similar shapes drawn efficiently, as `scatter` returns). Containers (`Figure`, `Axes`, `Axis`, `Tick`) hold other artists.

Every Artist shares an interface: `get_*`/`set_*` properties, `set(**kwargs)` for several at once, `set_visible`, `set_zorder` (drawing order), `set_alpha`, `set_clip_on`, `get_children()` and `findobj(match)` to search the subtree. `plt.getp(artist)` lists all properties, a quick way to discover what is settable.

Plotting helpers are just factories: `ax.bar` creates `Rectangle` patches and adds them with `ax.add_patch`. You can do the same, building custom shapes with `matplotlib.patches` and adding them yourself.

Artists only describe what to draw; nothing is rendered until the canvas draws the figure, calling each artist's `draw(renderer)` in z-order. That is why some values, such as text extents or automatic tick labels, are only accurate after `fig.canvas.draw()`.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
from matplotlib.text import Text

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(["a", "b", "c"], [3, 5, 2])
ax.set_title("Sales")

print(type(ax.patches[0]).__name__, len(ax.patches))  # Rectangle 3
ax.patches[1].set(color="tab:red", hatch="//")        # restyle one bar
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((-0.5, 4), 3, 0.1, color="gray", alpha=0.5))

texts = fig.findobj(Text)
print(any(t.get_text() == "Sales" for t in texts))   # True
for s in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
print([type(c).__name__ for c in ax.get_children()][:4])
# ['Rectangle', 'Rectangle', 'Rectangle', 'Rectangle']
fig.savefig("artists.png")
takeaways: Every drawn element is an Artist in a tree rooted at the Figure
All Artists share get/set properties, visibility, z-order and `findobj`
Plot functions create primitives you can later restyle or add yourself
pitfalls: Reading text sizes or tick labels before the figure has been drawn, and getting placeholder values.

quiz.q: A seaborn function returned an Axes, and you want to recolor just the second bar. Where is it?
quiz.explain: Bars are Rectangle patches stored in the Axes' patches list.

concepts.name: Coordinate systems and transforms
concepts.summary: Understand data, axes, figure and display coordinates and the transform pipeline that maps between them.
concepts.why: Placing elements precisely, such as insets, labels at fixed offsets or lines spanning panels, requires choosing the right coordinate system.
concepts.body:
Every artist has a **transform** mapping its coordinates to display pixels. The four you use most:

- `ax.transData`: data coordinates, the default for plotted data.
- `ax.transAxes`: (0, 0) is the Axes' bottom-left, (1, 1) its top-right.
- `fig.transFigure`: the same for the whole figure.
- `fig.dpi_scale_trans`: inches from the figure's bottom-left.

Pass any of them as `transform=` to text, patches or lines. Blended transforms mix systems per axis: `ax.get_xaxis_transform()` uses data x and axes y, so a span from y=0 to 1 always covers the full height at a given x (this is how `axvline` works).

Transforms compose with `+`. `transData` itself is `transScale + transLimits + transAxes`, which is how log scales and limits feed into pixels. `ScaledTranslation(dx, dy, fig.dpi_scale_trans)` adds an offset in inches, so `ax.transData + offset` places something a fixed physical distance from a data point regardless of zoom.

`transform.transform(points)` converts to display pixels and `transform.inverted()` goes back, for example to convert a mouse position or to compute where a label landed.

Display coordinates depend on figure size, dpi and limits, so compute them only after the layout is final (after a draw), and never store pixel positions across resizes. `ax.inset_axes([x, y, w, h])` uses axes coordinates by default, making insets resolution-independent.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.transforms as mtransforms

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3), dpi=100)
ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 100)

# data -> display pixels and back
px = ax.transData.transform((5, 50))
print(ax.transData.inverted().transform(px))   # [ 5. 50.]

# axes coordinates: centre of the Axes, whatever the limits
print((ax.transAxes.transform((0.5, 0.5)) == px).all())  # True here

# blended: x in data, y in axes -> full-height marker at x=7
trans = ax.get_xaxis_transform()
ax.plot([7, 7], [0, 1], transform=trans, color="red")

# fixed 10-point offset to the right of a data point
offset = mtransforms.ScaledTranslation(10 / 72, 0, fig.dpi_scale_trans)
ax.text(5, 50, "label", transform=ax.transData + offset)
print(ax.transData.contains_branch(ax.transAxes))   # True
fig.savefig("transforms.png")
takeaways: transData, transAxes, transFigure and dpi_scale_trans cover most needs
Blended transforms mix data and axes coordinates per axis
Compose with `+`; `inverted()` maps pixels back to data
pitfalls: Caching display coordinates before the final layout or dpi is applied.

quiz.q: You want a vertical marker at x = 3 (data) spanning the full height of the Axes whatever the y limits. Which transform fits?
quiz.explain: The x-axis transform blends data x with axes y, so y from 0 to 1 is always the full height.

concepts.name: Performance and large data
concepts.summary: Speed up rendering of big datasets and live plots with blitting, rasterization, simplification and decimation.
concepts.why: Plots with millions of points or real-time updates can take seconds per frame or produce huge files unless you know where the time goes.
concepts.body:
Rendering cost grows with the number of artists and vertices, so the big wins are drawing fewer, simpler things:

- **Use one artist, not many**: one `plot` call with many points is far faster than thousands of separate calls. For many line segments, use a `LineCollection`.
- **Prefer `plot(..., "o")` to `scatter`** when markers share one size and color.
- **Path simplification**: `path.simplify` (on by default) removes vertices that do not change the rendered line; `path.simplify_threshold` trades accuracy for speed. `agg.path.chunksize` (for example 10000) helps Agg with very long lines.
- **Marker subsampling**: `markevery=10` draws a marker every tenth point.
- **Decimate first**: for 10 million samples, aggregate (resample, `hexbin`, `hist2d`, datashader) to what the screen can show.

For vector output, `rasterized=True` on a dense artist embeds it as an image inside the SVG/PDF while text and axes stay vector, which keeps files small; `dpi` in `savefig` controls that image's resolution.

**Blitting** makes live updates fast: draw the static background once, cache it with `canvas.copy_from_bbox(fig.bbox)`, then for each frame `restore_region`, redraw only the changing artists with `ax.draw_artist`, and `canvas.blit`. Mark animated artists with `animated=True` so the normal draw skips them. `FuncAnimation(blit=True)` does exactly this.

Measure before optimizing: time `fig.canvas.draw()` and compare.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import time, os

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=200_000); y = rng.normal(size=200_000)

def timed_draw(fig):
    t = time.perf_counter(); fig.canvas.draw()
    return time.perf_counter() - t

fig1, ax1 = plt.subplots(); ax1.scatter(x, y, s=1)
fig2, ax2 = plt.subplots(); ax2.plot(x, y, ",", linestyle="none")
print(timed_draw(fig2) < timed_draw(fig1))  # True: one Line2D beats a collection

fig3, ax3 = plt.subplots(); ax3.plot(x, y, ",", linestyle="none", rasterized=True)
fig2.savefig("vector.pdf"); fig3.savefig("raster_inside.pdf", dpi=150)
print(os.path.getsize("raster_inside.pdf") < os.path.getsize("vector.pdf"))  # True
takeaways: Fewer artists and vertices is the main lever; aggregate huge data first
`rasterized=True` keeps vector files small for dense layers
Blitting redraws only changing artists over a cached background
pitfalls: Calling `plot` in a Python loop once per point, creating thousands of artists.

quiz.q: A PDF with a 500k-point scatter is 60 MB and slow to open. Which change keeps axes and text sharp but shrinks the file?
options: Pass rasterized=True to the scatter and save with a sensible dpi
quiz.explain: Rasterizing only the dense artist embeds it as an image while the rest of the PDF stays vector.
